The European flounder (Platichthys flesus) is a flatfish species widely distributed across coastal and estuarine waters of Europe. This species exhibits a maximum recorded total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], which is notably large among pleuronectids inhabiting temperate estuaries. Field surveys indicate that sexual maturation is initiated when individuals reach a length of 22.4 centimeters [Lp = 22.4 centimeters], a value that corresponds to the onset of gonadal recrudescence in both males and females. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva, emerging after the completion of embryonic development, possesses an extremely modest wet weight at birth of approximately 0.00052 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00052 grams], reflecting the small size of the pelagic egg from which it hatches. This minute initial mass is typical of flatfish species that produce large numbers of planktonic offspring as part of an r-selected reproductive strategy. The larval period is characterized by rapid growth and morphological transformation, culminating in a metamorphic climax that sees the migration of one eye to the opposite side of the body.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a constant 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], the onset of exogenous feeding occurs at 7 days [ab = 7 days], representing the brief interval between hatching and the commencement of independent feeding. This relatively short yolk-dependent phase is typical for marine teleosts with small yolk reserves. During this lecithotrophic stage, the prolarva relies entirely on endogenous nutrients absorbed from the yolk sac. The rapid progression from hatching to the onset of exogenous feeding is an important life-history trait that influences early survival rates and recruitment success in estuarine environments. At this same acclimation temperature, the maximum lifespan recorded in captivity reaches 15 years [am = 15 years], though wild populations typically exhibit shorter longevity due to predation and fishing pressure at a temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C]. This lifespan is substantial for a flatfish of moderate body size and suggests a relatively slow pace of senescence.

Reproductive output in Platichthys flesus is considerable, reflecting its life-history strategy as a batch spawner with high fecundity. Gravid females produce approximately 5,479 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 5,479 eggs per spawning event] when maintained at the thermal regime typical of their spring spawning season (10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C]). Field observations indicate that individual females complete approximately 365 spawning events each year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events each year], with the annual reproductive cycle closely synchronized with seasonal temperature and photoperiod cues. The combination of moderately large clutch size and near-daily spawning frequency yields a substantial lifetime reproductive output that compensates for the high mortality rates experienced during the pelagic larval phase. This iteroparous spawning strategy is common among pleuronectids and allows for the maintenance of stable populations despite unpredictable environmental conditions in estuarine nursery grounds. The reproductive biology of this species has been extensively studied in both the Baltic Sea and North Sea populations.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult European flounder has been estimated at approximately 2,200 grams [Wwi = approximately 2,200 grams], based on length-weight relationships derived from extensive sampling across multiple geographic populations. This asymptotic body mass corresponds to the maximum total length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] and indicates a robust, laterally compressed body form. Comparisons with congeneric species such as Platichthys stellatus reveal that P. flesus achieves a somewhat higher ultimate body mass relative to its maximum length, suggesting species-specific differences in allometric growth patterns. The relationship between length and mass is influenced by factors including habitat productivity, prey availability, and population density. Seasonal variation in body condition is well-documented, with individuals typically attaining their highest mass prior to the spawning season and experiencing a decline during the post-spawning period. This species demonstrates considerable phenotypic plasticity in growth trajectories across its broad geographic range.

The maximum reproductive rate observed in this species, calculated as approximately 5,479 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 5,479 eggs per day] when measured at the species' optimal spawning temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], underscores the high fecundity that characterizes this flatfish. This daily fecundity value, derived from field studies of ovarian development and batch fecundity, represents the peak output achievable under favorable thermal and nutritional conditions. The pelagic eggs, each measuring approximately 1 millimeter in diameter, are released into the water column where they undergo external fertilisation and subsequent development. The successful recruitment of these larvae is highly dependent on the timing of spawning relative to the spring bloom of zooplankton prey. Estuarine habitats serve as critical nursery grounds where juvenile flounder benefit from abundant food resources and reduced predation pressure, facilitating rapid growth toward the length at puberty of 22.4 centimeters [Lp = 22.4 centimeters].
